propositions.text: Justice rendered in secret risks rule of law and public confidence; open court principle guards democracy and ensures judicial accountability.
propositions.quote: When justice is rendered in secret, without leaving any trace, respect for the rule of law is jeopardized and public confidence in the administration of justice may be shaken.

propositions.text: Open court principle supports impartial, fair justice and enhances public understanding and confidence in the justice system.
propositions.quote: The open court principle allows a society to guard against such risks, which erode the very foundations of democracy.

propositions.text: Court openness is constitutionally protected in Canada and is paramount to democracy.
propositions.quote: Court openness is therefore of paramount importance to our democracy — an importance that is also reflected in the constitutional protection afforded to it in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds secret justice risks rule of law and public confidence; open court principle is constitutionally protected and vital to democracy.

propositions.text: Case about Named Person, a police informer convicted after a so-called 'secret trial', caused public concern and indignation.
propositions.quote: In this context, it is therefore hardly surprising that this case concerning Named Person, a police informer who, according to the Court of Appeal, was convicted following a “secret trial”, has provoked both concern and indignation among the public.

propositions.text: The idea of secret trials with no trace is intolerable and contrary to Canadian democratic ideals.
propositions.quote: The very idea that “secret trials” — that is, criminal proceedings of which no trace exists — may be conducted in our liberal democracy is indeed an intolerable one.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the case about Named Person's alleged secret trial caused public concern; secret trials are intolerable and anti-democratic.

propositions.text: Controversy arose after Court of Appeal's March 2022 judgment denounced a 'secret trial' using unfortunate expression.
propositions.quote: The controversy, which arose after the Court of Appeal released a judgment in March 2022 in which it misguidedly denounced the holding of a “secret trial”, was largely due to the gap between what the public knew and what it did not know, combined with the effect of the unfortunate expression used by the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Expression suggested Named Person was convicted after a secret proceeding, alarming public and media and harming confidence.
propositions.quote: That expression could in fact have suggested that Named Person had been convicted following a secret criminal proceeding.

propositions.text: No secret trial was held; proceeding was public until Named Person filed a motion for stay based on abusive state conduct.
propositions.quote: But to be clear, no secret trial was held in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains controversy arose from Court of Appeal's wording suggesting a secret trial, but no secret trial occurred; proceeding was public until stay motion.

propositions.text: 'Secret trial' concept does not exist in Canada; court openness can be limited by confidentiality orders but not to the extent of secret trials.
propositions.quote: In fact, the very concept of “secret trial” does not exist in Canada.

propositions.text: Comparing fully in camera hearings to secret trials is wrong and unnecessarily alarming.
propositions.quote: any comparison of hearings held totally in camera to a “secret trial” is wrong and needlessly alarming.

paragraphs.summary: The court states secret trials do not exist in Canada; full in camera hearings are not secret trials and such comparisons are wrong and alarming.

propositions.text: Appeals provide opportunity to clarify facts, reassure public, and reaffirm open justice importance.
propositions.quote: These appeals therefore provide this Court with an opportunity to set the record straight, to reassure the public and to reaffirm the importance of ensuring that justice is administered openly and transparently.

propositions.text: Court will reiterate Named Person v. Vancouver Sun procedure and rule protecting informer privilege while minimizing open court impairment.
propositions.quote: First, the appeals allow the Court to reiterate the relevance of the procedure set out in Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43...

paragraphs.summary: The court says appeals allow it to clarify facts, reassure public, and reaffirm open justice and informer privilege protection rules.

propositions.text: Appeals show excesses when Vancouver Sun rule is not rigorously applied in in camera proceedings.
propositions.quote: Second, the appeals illustrate the excesses that may occur when the guiding rule from Vancouver Sun is not rigorously applied at the stage of conducting in camera proceedings.

propositions.text: Trial judges should create parallel sealed proceedings separate from public trial when protecting informer identity by total in camera proceedings.
propositions.quote: he would have created a parallel proceeding separate from the one in which Named Person had invoked informer privilege.

propositions.text: Parallel proceeding record, though sealed, should have its own docket number and public redacted judgment could be released.
propositions.quote: The record for the parallel proceeding thereby created, though sealed, would have had its own number.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appeals show excesses from not rigorously applying Vancouver Sun; trial judges should create parallel sealed proceedings with public redacted judgments.

propositions.text: Named Person charged with criminal offences and moved for stay of proceedings based on abusive state conduct and unreasonable trial delay.
propositions.quote: Named Person, a police informer, was charged with criminal offences. As their only defence, Named Person brought a motion for a stay of proceedings based both on the infringement of their right to be protected from any abusive state conduct...

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Named Person charged and moved for stay based on abusive state conduct and unreasonable delay.

propositions.text: First in camera hearing verified Named Person's informer status; judge ordered motion for stay to be heard in camera with no media notice.
propositions.quote: A first in camera hearing was held to verify Named Person’s status as a police informer... judge ordered that the motion for a stay of proceedings be heard in camera.

propositions.text: Motion, exhibits, and transcripts remained confidential and were not listed in any docket.
propositions.quote: The motion, its content and the exhibits and transcripts submitted to the judge remained confidential and were not listed in any docket.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge held in camera hearing confirming informer status and ordered stay motion heard in camera with confidentiality and no media notice.

propositions.text: Motion for stay dismissed; no evidence state acted abusively or unreasonable delay occurred; judgment had no file number and was not public.
propositions.quote: The motion for a stay of proceedings was dismissed. In the trial judge’s view, it could not be concluded from the record that the state had acted abusively... That judgment had no file number and... was not public.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge dismissed stay motion for lack of abusive state conduct or delay; judgment was confidential and unnumbered.

propositions.text: Named Person convicted and appealed on ground trial judge erred in not finding abusive state conduct; appeal did not concern delay or informer privilege.
propositions.quote: Named Person was subsequently convicted. They decided to appeal the conviction on the ground that the trial judge had erred in declining to find that the state had acted abusively...

paragraphs.summary: Named Person appealed conviction alleging trial judge erred on abusive state conduct; appeal did not address delay or informer privilege.

propositions.text: On appeal, parties requested in camera proceedings; Court of Appeal agreed and referred public access question to merits panel; no media notice given.
propositions.quote: On appeal, the parties asked that the proceedings remain in camera. The Court of Appeal agreed to their request... no notice was given to the media.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal held appeal in camera on parties' request and deferred public access question; no media notice given.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal allowed appeal, stayed conviction and proceedings for state abuse of process; criticized police for inadequate informing of Named Person.
propositions.quote: On February 28, 2022, in a unanimous judgment, the Court of Appeal allowed Named Person’s appeal, stayed the conviction and entered a stay of the criminal proceedings on the ground of abuse of process by the state.

propositions.text: Police failed to inform Named Person of limits and consequences of cooperation, leading to unfair trial and undermining justice integrity.
propositions.quote: The failure to adequately inform Named Person... had led Named Person to believe that they had to admit all of the facts...

propositions.text: State conduct compromised trial fairness, judicial integrity, and discouraged police informers.
propositions.quote: Such state conduct compromised the fairness of the trial and undermined the integrity of the judicial process, in addition to discouraging persons from providing information to the police.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal stayed conviction for state abuse, criticized police for inadequate informing, compromising fairness and judicial integrity.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal disagreed with confidentiality scope, condemning 'secret trial' with no trace as contrary to legal principles and democracy.
propositions.quote: It found that, as important as informer privilege may be, it cannot justify holding a trial of which no trace exists...

propositions.text: Trial must be public subject to specific non-publication or partial in camera orders; secretive proceedings violate constitutional and media rights.
propositions.quote: the trial itself must be public, subject to specific non‑publication orders or partial in camera orders

propositions.text: Court of Appeal opened a sealed record and made public a redacted judgment version of February 28, 2022 decision.
propositions.quote: For this reason, the Court of Appeal decided to open a record at its court office, accompanied by a sealing order, and to make public a redacted version of its judgment of February 28, 2022.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal condemned secret trial, affirmed trial must be public with limited exceptions, and released redacted judgment publicly.

propositions.text: On March 23, 2022, Court of Appeal released judgment with extensive redactions to protect Named Person's identity and related details.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal released a version of its judgment in which the following information was redacted: Named Person’s name; the identity of the trial court and judge;...

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal released redacted judgment protecting Named Person's identity and related information.

propositions.text: Public interpreted Court of Appeal's preliminary remarks as revealing a secret criminal proceeding leading to conviction, causing shock and incomprehension.
propositions.quote: The public understood them as revealing the conduct of a secret criminal proceeding that had led to Named Person’s conviction.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds public misunderstood Court of Appeal's remarks as revealing a secret trial, causing shock.

propositions.text: Appellants and intervener requested Court of Appeal to review and lift or limit confidentiality orders in Named Person's case.
propositions.quote: Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. asked the Court of Appeal to review the confidentiality orders made in Named Person’s case...

paragraphs.summary: Appellants and intervener requested Court of Appeal review and lift or limit confidentiality orders.

propositions.text: On July 20, 2022, Court of Appeal dismissed motions to review confidentiality orders and upheld sealing of information identifying Named Person.
propositions.quote: On July 20, 2022... the Court of Appeal dismissed the motions brought by the appellants and the intervener Rondeau for review of the confidentiality orders and upheld the sealing of all information that might tend to identify Named Person.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal dismissed motions to review confidentiality orders and upheld sealing of identifying information.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found Named Person indisputably a police informer entitled to privilege; appellants did not contest this.
propositions.quote: it was indisputable that Named Person was a police informer and was entitled to the privilege attaching to that status... something that the appellants and the intervener Rondeau did not contest.

propositions.text: No disclosure of information that might identify Named Person is possible without endangering them, including personal and case details.
propositions.quote: there was no possibility of disclosing any information that might tend to identify Named Person, at the risk of endangering them...

propositions.text: Even identities of judge, court, prosecutor, counsel, police force must be kept confidential to protect Named Person's identity.
propositions.quote: it was also impermissible in this case to reveal the identity of the judge, the trial court, the judicial district, the prosecutor and counsel for the prosecution, counsel for Named Person and the police force involved.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal found Named Person's informer privilege indisputable and upheld broad confidentiality to protect identity.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal rejected partial unsealing of appeal record as impracticable due to duty to preserve informer privilege and risk of error.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal also rejected the alternative argument that it should have partially unsealed the appeal record by redacting the same information as in the public version of the judgment...

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal rejected partial unsealing of record as impracticable and risky for informer privilege preservation.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal has no inherent jurisdiction to set aside confidentiality orders made by trial court unless on appeal.
propositions.quote: a court of appeal, unlike a superior court, has no inherent jurisdiction... it cannot review orders made by another court unless they are before it on appeal...

propositions.text: Court of Appeal criticized trial confidentiality measures but lacked jurisdiction to vary trial judge's orders.
propositions.quote: the fact that, in its judgment on the appeal, [a court of appeal] criticized the manner of proceeding at trial... does not mean that it acquired jurisdiction to correct or vary the trial judge’s orders.

propositions.text: Appellants' inability to act does not give Court of Appeal jurisdiction to review trial court confidentiality orders; this aspect not appealed.
propositions.quote: the fact that this situation put the appellants in a position where it was impossible to act could not give the Court of Appeal jurisdiction to review the confidentiality orders made by the trial court.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal lacks jurisdiction to set aside trial court confidentiality orders; criticism does not confer jurisdiction; this issue not appealed.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal implicitly recognized it was wrong to use 'secret trial' and stopped using the expression.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal implicitly recognized that it had been wrong in using the expression “secret trial” in its preliminary remarks and that the expression had caused undue concern among the public

propositions.text: Court of Appeal linked in camera proceedings and confidentiality measures to the motion for a stay of proceedings.
propositions.quote: now also clearly linked the in camera proceedings ordered without notice to the media, as well as the other confidentiality measures taken at trial, to the motion for a stay of proceedings

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal admitted it was wrong to call it a 'secret trial' and linked confidentiality measures to the stay of proceedings motion, as found by the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: The appeals raise three questions about Vancouver Sun procedure, its application in camera, and Court of Appeal's refusal to vary confidentiality orders.
propositions.quote: The appeals raise the following questions: 1. Should the procedure set out in Vancouver Sun be modified to make it more consistent with the open court principle? 2. How is the guiding rule from Vancouver Sun to be applied when proceeding in camera? 3. Did the Court of Appeal err in refusing to vary or set aside its confidentiality orders?

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the three issues raised on appeal regarding Vancouver Sun procedure, its application, and Court of Appeal's confidentiality orders.

propositions.text: The procedure proposed in Vancouver Sun should not be modified as changes are unnecessary and undesirable.
propositions.quote: the procedure proposed in Vancouver Sun should not be modified. In addition to departing from well‑settled jurisprudence, the changes proposed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. are not necessary or even desirable.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes Vancouver Sun procedure should not be modified as proposed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al.

propositions.text: Applying Vancouver Sun's guiding rule ensures public knowledge of in camera hearings and judgments, possibly via parallel sealed proceedings.
propositions.quote: the application of the guiding rule from Vancouver Sun ... will necessarily ensure that ... the existence of an in camera hearing and of any judgment rendered as a result will be made public ... it may be necessary to create a parallel proceeding ... The record for the parallel proceeding ... will then have its own record number ... it will generally be possible for the proceeding to be on the court’s docket and hearing roll and for a public judgment to be released.

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds Vancouver Sun's guiding rule ensures public knowledge of in camera hearings and judgments, possibly via parallel sealed proceedings.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal did not shield non-confidential information but erred in sealing entire appeal record; a redacted trial judgment should be public.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal, in its redacted reasons, did not shield non‑confidential information from public view ... the Court of Appeal erred in upholding its order that the entire appeal record be sealed. It should have made a redacted version of the trial judgment public.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Court of Appeal did not shield non-confidential info but erred in sealing entire record; redacted trial judgment should be public.

propositions.text: Analysis begins with reviewing open court principle and informer privilege rules.
propositions.quote: It will be helpful to begin the analysis by reviewing the importance of the open court principle and the rules surrounding informer privilege.

paragraphs.summary: The Court begins analysis by reviewing the open court principle and informer privilege rules.

propositions.text: Open court principle is constitutionally protected and a pillar of free and democratic society.
propositions.quote: This Court has repeatedly affirmed that the open court principle, which is protected by the constitutionally entrenched right of freedom of expression, is a pillar of our free and democratic society

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the open court principle is constitutionally protected and a pillar of democracy.

propositions.text: Open court principle includes public hearings and records, and right to report on proceedings.
propositions.quote: The open court principle has two aspects: first, the public nature of hearings and court records, and second, the right to report on court proceedings.

propositions.text: Under open court principle, everyone generally has right to access courts, attend hearings, consult records, and report.
propositions.quote: Under this principle, every person, as a general rule, has the right to access the courts, to attend hearings, to consult court records and to report on their content

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the open court principle includes public hearings, records, and reporting rights, citing prior authorities.

propositions.text: Open court principle with free media ensures judicial accountability, independence, fairness, and public confidence.
propositions.quote: Coupled with the existence of free, robust and independent news media, the open court principle performs a number of important social and democratic functions ... it promotes both judicial independence and an administration of justice that is impartial, fair and in accordance with the rule of law ... enhances public confidence in the integrity of the justice system

propositions.text: Open justice facilitates public understanding and confidence in justice system and participants.
propositions.quote: Open justice also facilitates the public’s understanding of the administration of justice and enhances public confidence in the integrity of the justice system and all of its participants

paragraphs.summary: The Court states open court principle with free media promotes judicial accountability, independence, fairness, and public confidence.

propositions.text: Open court principle ensures accountability of justice system and its actors, maintaining legitimacy and fairness.
propositions.quote: The very legitimacy of the legal system depends on “public acceptance of process and outcome,” and the open court system promotes this acceptance by ensuring the accountability of the justice system ... Transparency ... acts as a “powerful disinfectant” ... open court principle ... assures the public accountability of the court system and its key actors

propositions.text: Open court principle supports accountability beyond judges, including police and warrants, ensuring fair trials.
propositions.quote: It is not just judges who are presumably held to account by the open court principle. The principle is also said to support positive results with respect to other justice system players and functions outside of the courtroom ... The openness of trials has been held to be an expression of the judge’s confidence that what happens in the courtroom is “beyond reproach.”

propositions.text: Open court principle maintains and enhances public confidence and integrity of justice system and participants.
propositions.quote: Their comments clearly underscore how court openness helps to maintain and enhance public confidence in, and serves “in a way as a guarantee of”, the integrity of the justice system, including all of its participants

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites authorities explaining open court principle ensures accountability, fairness, and public confidence in justice system.

propositions.text: Free, robust, independent media is essential for open justice to serve social and democratic functions.
propositions.quote: When it comes to the social and democratic functions of the open court principle, the key role played by the news media cannot be overemphasized ... it is the media that serve as “the eyes and ears of a wider public which would be absolutely entitled to attend [proceedings under way] but for purely practical reasons cannot do so”

propositions.text: Media enables public understanding, opinion, accountability, and confidence in justice system.
propositions.quote: It is only the presence of free, robust and independent news media that actually enables the public to understand and form an opinion on the justice system, to hold it accountable and to have confidence in it

paragraphs.summary: The Court emphasizes media's key role in enabling public understanding, accountability, and confidence in justice system.

propositions.text: Confidentiality orders limiting court openness are rare exceptions justified only when ends of justice require.
propositions.quote: Because of the fundamental importance of court openness, confidentiality orders limiting it can be made by the courts only in rare circumstances ... openness cannot prevail if the ends of justice ... would be better served in some other way

propositions.text: Informer privilege is one such exception to open court principle.
propositions.quote: One of these exceptions is informer privilege, which is the one in question in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states confidentiality orders limiting openness are rare exceptions, including informer privilege.

propositions.text: Informer privilege protects identity of those giving confidential criminal information to police.
propositions.quote: Informer privilege is a “judicially created ‘rule of public policy’ designed to further the ends of law enforcement” ... protects from revelation ... the identity of those who give information related to criminal matters in confidence

propositions.text: Informer privilege applies when police receive information under promise of confidentiality, implicit or explicit.
propositions.quote: It applies whenever it is established that the police have received information under a promise of confidentiality, whether implicit or explicit

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains informer privilege protects identities of confidential criminal informants, applying when police receive info under confidentiality promise.

propositions.text: The Court will explain rationale, exception to open court principle, and broad scope of informer privilege.
propositions.quote: It will be helpful to briefly explain (1) the rationale for this privilege, (2) how it forms an exception to the open court principle and (3) its broad scope.

paragraphs.summary: The Court will explain rationale, exception to open court principle, and broad scope of informer privilege.

propositions.text: Informer privilege furthers law enforcement by protecting informers who face retribution risk, benefiting public order.
propositions.quote: Informer privilege is granted in the public interest ... Informers pass on useful information ... They thus play a critical role ... Informers often face the risk of retribution ... informer privilege was developed to protect the identity ... By protecting those who assist the police ... the privilege furthers the interests of justice and the maintenance of public order

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites authority explaining informer privilege protects informers to further law enforcement and public order.

propositions.text: Informer privilege is granted not for informer’s interest but for effective law enforcement and public order.
propositions.quote: the social justification for this privilege [is] found in the need to ensure performance of the policing function and maintenance of law and order ... granted not in the interest of the informer, “but in the interest of more effective law enforcement”

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites authority that informer privilege serves law enforcement and public order, not informer's interest.

propositions.text: Informer privilege is absolute or near absolute and non-discretionary; no balancing of interests allowed once established.
propositions.quote: Informer privilege is of such importance that it has repeatedly been characterized as “absolute” or “near absolute” ... once informer status is established, courts are not permitted to weigh ... competing legitimate interests

propositions.text: Privilege applies regardless of risk to informer, pursuit of truth, or public confidence preservation.
propositions.quote: courts are not permitted to weigh the maintenance or scope of the privilege on a case‑by‑case basis ... such as the level of risk faced by the informer, the pursuit of truth or the preservation of public confidence in the administration of justice

paragraphs.summary: The Court states informer privilege is absolute and non-discretionary, disallowing balancing of competing interests once established.

propositions.text: Informer privilege applies in all proceedings with one narrow criminal law exception to establish innocence.
propositions.quote: The informer privilege rule applies in civil, administrative and criminal proceedings and admits but one exception, under the criminal law, in cases where this is “necessary to establish innocence in a criminal trial”

propositions.text: The exception is narrow and distinct from accused’s broader right to full answer and defence.
propositions.quote: The exception is a narrow one that is distinct from the broader right of an accused to make full answer and defence

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains informer privilege applies broadly with a narrow exception to establish innocence in criminal trials.

propositions.text: Informer privilege belongs to Crown and informer; neither can waive without other's consent.
propositions.quote: This privilege belongs “both to the Crown and to the informer and neither can waive it without the consent of the other”

propositions.text: Police, Crown, and courts must keep informer identity confidential; privilege circle is limited.
propositions.quote: police, the Crown and the courts have a duty to keep the identity of informers confidential ... courts have refused to widen to include ... defence counsel or the syndic of the Barreau du Québec

paragraphs.summary: The Court states informer privilege belongs to Crown and informer, and police, Crown, courts must keep identity confidential.

propositions.text: Courts have no discretion to disclose informer identity even if limiting privilege would allow more complete justice.
propositions.quote: the duty to keep a police informer’s identity confidential means that they do not have “any discretion to disclose ... information ... even where limiting the scope of the privilege ... would allow “more complete justice” to be done

propositions.text: Privilege applies automatically and judges must ensure respect for it on their own motion.
propositions.quote: The application of the privilege is not subject to any formal requirement, and judges must even ensure respect for it of their own motion

propositions.text: Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. argued Dagenais/Mentuck test helps limit informer privilege discretion.
propositions.quote: contrary to the arguments made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. (A.F., at paras. 68 and 79), the test developed in Dagenais ... and R. v. Mentuck ... and reformulated in Sherman is of no assistance

propositions.text: Dagenais/Mentuck test does not assist because judges have no discretion once informer privilege applies.
propositions.quote: a judge has no discretion once it is shown that informer privilege applies

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds courts have no discretion to disclose informer identity; rejects Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's argument that Dagenais/Mentuck test limits privilege.

propositions.text: Non-discretionary privileges must take precedence over public order or interest, with limited exceptions.
propositions.quote: non‑discretionary privileges must [translation] “take precedence over any other consideration, even of public order or public interest, with some limited exceptions” (2022 QCCA 984, at para. 53).

propositions.text: Informer privilege is absolute, applies without regard to case facts, and harm is presumed.
propositions.quote: It is a privilege that produces its effects “without regard to the particulars of the situation” (thus without regard to the facts of each case) and without it being necessary to establish harm, which is in fact presumed

propositions.text: Informer privilege differs from case-by-case privileges requiring balancing interests and proof of necessity.
propositions.quote: this is how it differs from privilege recognized on a case‑by‑case basis, which calls for such a balancing of the interests of those who claim confidentiality and must show that it is necessary against the interests of those who oppose it or seek access to information.

propositions.text: Informer privilege is absolute and excludes weighing public interest conflicts, as explained by Beetz J. in Bisaillon.
propositions.quote: the law gives the Minister, and the Court after him, no power of weighing or evaluating various aspects of the public interest which are in conflict, since it has already resolved the conflict itself.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found informer privilege absolute, overriding public interest, differing from case-by-case privileges, citing Beetz J. in Bisaillon.

propositions.text: Informer privilege is virtually absolute and overrides the open court principle despite societal costs.
propositions.quote: recognition of the non‑discretionary and thus virtually absolute nature of informer privilege means that the interests protected by the open court principle yield to those protected by informer privilege.

propositions.text: This choice may override important public interests but is essential for police investigations and public protection.
propositions.quote: it is a choice that is essential in guaranteeing the effectiveness of police investigations, the maintenance of public order and the protection of the Canadian public.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds informer privilege overrides open court principle, essential despite societal trade-offs for police and public protection.

propositions.text: Informer privilege is extremely broad, covering identity and any information leading to identification, including testimony and documents.
propositions.quote: informer privilege is extremely broad in its application. It applies “to the identity of every informer... and even where the informer himself or herself is a witness”, and it applies “to both documentary evidence and oral testimony”

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds informer privilege broadly covers identity and any information that might identify the informer.

propositions.text: Courts must exercise caution to keep confidential any information that might identify the informer, considering the informer's network context.
propositions.quote: any information — even the smallest detail — that may lead directly or indirectly to the identification of the informer must be kept confidential

propositions.text: Informer privilege protects both the informer from retribution and signals protection to potential informers.
propositions.quote: the ban on revealing the informer’s identity protect that informer from possible retribution, it also sends a signal to potential informers that their identity, too, will be protected

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds courts must cautiously protect all information that might identify informers, safeguarding their safety and encouraging informers.

propositions.text: In criminal proceedings, informers are usually third parties providing police information, not accused persons.
propositions.quote: the informer is generally not themself an accused but rather a third party who has provided the police with information

propositions.text: Informer privilege arises indirectly, e.g., during Crown disclosure or police testimony about investigative steps.
propositions.quote: the question of informer privilege thus arises indirectly in the proceeding, for example at the stage of Crown disclosure or when a police officer being questioned about what led them to take a certain step invokes this privilege

propositions.text: Even small details can reveal informer identity, justifying a principle of caution from the criminal circle's perspective.
propositions.quote: [t]he tiniest and most seemingly innocuous of details could reveal the identity of an informer... which also provides further justification for the principle of caution based on the perspective of those in the same criminal circle as the informer

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds informer privilege arises indirectly in criminal cases and small details can reveal informer identity, requiring caution.

propositions.text: All details risking informer safety must be confidential; if uncertain, information should be kept confidential.
propositions.quote: all details — even those that would seem the most innocuous... must be kept confidential to the extent that their disclosure risks jeopardizing the informer’s safety

propositions.text: When identification risk is unclear, the principle of caution requires confidentiality of informer information.
propositions.quote: where it is difficult or impossible to identify the information that might compromise the informer’s anonymity, the principle of caution requires that the information provided by the informer be kept confidential

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds all details risking informer safety must be confidential, applying caution when identification risk is unclear.

propositions.text: Vancouver Sun established a flexible procedure balancing informer privilege and open court principle.
propositions.quote: this Court addressed the relationship between the openness of court proceedings and informer privilege. It proposed a procedure... giving full effect to the requirements of this “privilege which is extremely broad and powerful”

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes Vancouver Sun created a flexible procedure balancing informer privilege and open court principle.

propositions.text: The procedure has two stages: first, verify privilege via in camera, ex parte hearing with limited attendance.
propositions.quote: the court must verify the existence of the privilege. For this purpose, it will hold an in camera hearing that, if necessary, will be ex parte

propositions.text: At stage one, claim of informer privilege must not be disclosed; only privilege holders and limited persons may attend.
propositions.quote: “even the claim of informer privilege must not be disclosed”... only the police informer and the Crown... may attend the hearing

propositions.text: Judge must be satisfied on balance that person is a confidential informer; no discretion to deny privilege once evidence is shown.
propositions.quote: the judge’s responsibility at this stage is “to demand from the parties some evidence which satisfies the judge, on balance, that the person is a confidential informer”... the judge has no discretion in this regard

propositions.text: Informer privilege is a rule of public order, automatically engaged by evidence of informer status.
propositions.quote: This is a rule of public order (Leipert, at para. 13, quoting Bisaillon, at p. 93).

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains stage one of Vancouver Sun procedure: confidential in camera hearing to verify informer privilege without discretion to deny it.

propositions.text: Stage two: after establishing privilege, court proceeds without violating privilege, balancing open court, right to be heard, adversarial nature.
propositions.quote: judge is charged with carrying on the proceedings without violating the privilege while at the same time accommodating... the open court principle, the right to be heard and the adversarial nature of the proceedings

propositions.text: Court determines appropriate confidentiality measures, may allow third party submissions or appoint amicus curiae for guidance.
propositions.quote: court will determine the appropriate measures to protect informer privilege... may consider it advisable to appoint an amicus curiae

propositions.text: Court should disclose as much information as possible to third parties or amicus without compromising informer anonymity.
propositions.quote: the court should... disclose as much information as possible to the third parties or the amicus curiae... No information... that might compromise the informer’s anonymity can be disclosed

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes stage two of Vancouver Sun: balancing privilege protection and open court, allowing third party input without revealing informer identity.

propositions.text: If court issues public notice inviting third party submissions, it must hear their arguments on confidentiality orders.
propositions.quote: If the court decides to issue a public notice... the judge will then have to hear their submissions in order to determine what confidentiality orders are appropriate

propositions.text: Media is granted standing to argue on respecting informer privilege with minimal open court impact.
propositions.quote: it is at this point that “the media is granted standing to present arguments on how informer privilege can be respected with minimal effect on the open court principle”

paragraphs.summary: The Court states that if a public notice is issued, media may present arguments on confidentiality orders protecting informer privilege.

propositions.text: Confidentiality orders vary by case, depending on informer's role and participation in proceedings.
propositions.quote: the appropriate confidentiality orders will vary with the circumstances of each case... depends on... the nature and extent of the informer’s participation

propositions.text: Court of Appeal noted confidentiality needs vary if informer testifies or is central to the case.
propositions.quote: the protection required may vary based, among other things, on whether or not they testify... or whether the individual and their informer status are at the centre of the case

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds confidentiality orders depend on case circumstances and informer's role, as noted by the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. argue Vancouver Sun's second stage should be modified to better align with open court principle.
propositions.quote: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. argue that it is time to modify this second stage of the Vancouver Sun procedure to make it more consistent with the open court principle

propositions.text: They say current cases reveal shortcomings and call to limit or eliminate judge's discretion and ease disclosure restrictions.
propositions.quote: they submit that these cases demonstrate the need to limit or even eliminate the judge’s discretion and also to ease restrictions on the disclosure of information

paragraphs.summary: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. argue to modify Vancouver Sun's second stage to reduce judge discretion and ease disclosure restrictions.

propositions.text: They ask to make judge's discretion a duty to notify interested third parties about informer privilege claims and confidentiality arguments.
propositions.quote: the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. first ask that this Court transform what has so far been the judge’s discretion to hear interested third parties on confidentiality orders into a duty to do so

propositions.text: They want a notice to media advising informer privilege claimed and arguments on protection measures forthcoming.
propositions.quote: a duty be imposed on the presiding judge to issue a notice to interested third parties, and principally the media, advising them that informer privilege has been claimed

propositions.text: They argue this duty ensures cases are never removed from public view again.
propositions.quote: transforming the judge’s discretion into a duty in this manner is the only way to ensure that a case is never again [translation] “removed from the view” of the public

propositions.text: They propose disclosing all non-identifying information to third parties or counsel with confidentiality undertakings, or at least informing them of nature and reasons for confidentiality.
propositions.quote: all information that does not directly identify the informer should be disclosed to interested third parties, or at least to their counsel, possibly with undertakings of confidentiality

paragraphs.summary: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. propose mandatory notice to third parties and broader disclosure of non-identifying information with confidentiality safeguards.

propositions.text: The Court disagrees with proposed changes, finding them unnecessary, undesirable, and departing from settled law.
propositions.quote: With respect, we disagree. In addition to departing from well‑settled jurisprudence, the changes called for are not necessary or even desirable.

paragraphs.summary: The Court disagrees with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al.'s proposed changes as unnecessary and departing from settled law.

propositions.text: Judges must retain discretion to decide if issuing notice to third parties is in interests of justice.
propositions.quote: it is imperative that judges have the discretion to determine whether it is in the interests of justice to issue a notice to interested third parties

propositions.text: Issuing notice is generally presumed in interests of justice but may be inappropriate if privilege holder is present and active in court.
propositions.quote: While it can be presumed that issuing a notice will generally be in the interests of justice, it is always possible that doing so will not be appropriate in a particular case

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds judges must keep discretion to issue notice to third parties, generally presumed appropriate but not always.

propositions.text: Vancouver Sun majority rejected mandatory notice to third parties when confidentiality orders are contemplated.
propositions.quote: a majority of this Court considered and rejected the idea that issuing a notice to interested third parties becomes mandatory where the making of confidentiality orders is being contemplated

propositions.text: No constitutional right exists to be informed of all informer privilege claims; discretion justified by practical considerations.
propositions.quote: no one has a right, constitutional or otherwise, to be informed of all situations in which informer privilege is claimed

propositions.text: It would be unworkable to require publicizing every in camera proceeding; discretion avoids this.
propositions.quote: It would be unworkable and unreasonable to expect that literally every time an in camera proceeding is taking place, a judge has the obligation to publicize its existence

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites Vancouver Sun rejecting mandatory notice to third parties, emphasizing discretion and practicality.

propositions.text: C.B.C. v. Manitoba affirms discretion in giving prior notice of limits on court openness.
propositions.quote: whether and when this notice should be given is ultimately a matter within the discretion of the relevant court

propositions.text: Courts have discretionary authority to ensure justice in each case regarding limits on court openness.
propositions.quote: courts have the requisite discretionary authority to ensure justice is served in each individual case

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites C.B.C. v. Manitoba affirming courts' discretion in prior notice of court openness limits.

propositions.text: No reason to depart from precedents preserving discretion to issue public notice limiting court openness.
propositions.quote: There is no reason to depart from these precedents... which unequivocally recognizes the importance of preserving the courts’ discretion to issue a public notice

propositions.text: Anecdotal misapplications do not justify overturning precedent or eroding stare decisis.
propositions.quote: Anecdotal examples of the misapplication... cannot on their own justify altering well‑settled jurisprudence

paragraphs.summary: The Court refuses to overturn precedent preserving discretion to issue public notice, rejecting anecdotal misapplication arguments.

propositions.text: The Court agrees with attorneys general that discretion to issue notice is necessary and desirable to serve justice.
propositions.quote: we agree with the attorneys general of Canada and Ontario that it is necessary and desirable for the courts to have the discretion to decide whether issuing a notice to interested third parties is in the interests of justice

propositions.text: Rigid mandatory notice could risk breaching informer privilege; discretion provides needed flexibility.
propositions.quote: one cannot exclude the possibility that a rigid rule would prevent an informer’s anonymity from being preserved

propositions.text: Notice should only be withheld exceptionally in best interests of justice.
propositions.quote: it is only exceptionally that the best interests of justice will require that no notice be given to the public

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds discretion to issue notice is necessary to protect informer privilege and serve justice, with exceptions rare.

propositions.text: The Court rejects argument to disclose non-identifying privileged information to third parties or their counsel.
propositions.quote: This Court is also unable to accept the argument... that any information that does not directly identify the informer should be disclosed to interested third parties

propositions.text: Disclosure to counsel with confidentiality undertakings does not change the need to protect privilege.
propositions.quote: The possibility of disclosing such information only to counsel... changes nothing in this regard

paragraphs.summary: The Court rejects disclosing non-identifying privileged information to third parties or their counsel, maintaining protection.

propositions.text: All information that might directly or indirectly identify the informer must be kept confidential.
propositions.quote: all information — even the most innocuous — that might tend to directly or indirectly identify the informer must be kept confidential.

propositions.text: A position that treats direct and indirect identifying information differently is rejected by jurisprudence.
propositions.quote: the creation of such a hierarchy for these two types of information has been rejected in our jurisprudence

paragraphs.summary: The court states all information identifying informers must be confidential and rejects any hierarchy between direct and indirect identification.

propositions.text: Judges must be extremely careful in disclosing information to third parties, limiting disclosure to non-identifying information only.
propositions.quote: a judge “must be extremely careful” when considering what information to disclose to interested third parties

propositions.text: No identifying information can be given to the media under any circumstances.
propositions.quote: no identifying information can be given to the media under any circumstances

propositions.text: Disclosure of privileged information, even with confidentiality undertakings, expands privilege circle and undermines informer privilege objectives.
propositions.quote: disclosure of such privileged information, even subject to undertakings of confidentiality, would unduly expand the circle of privilege

paragraphs.summary: The court cites prior authority that judges must limit disclosure to non-identifying information and avoid expanding privilege improperly.

propositions.text: CBC et al.'s position conflicts with Vancouver Sun and Basi decisions on informer privilege.
propositions.quote: the position stated by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. conflicts not only with this Court’s pronouncements in Vancouver Sun but also with those in Basi

propositions.text: Informer privilege cannot be lifted for defence counsel merely because of confidentiality undertakings, even if it supports constitutional rights.
propositions.quote: informer privilege cannot be lifted in favour of defence counsel merely because they are bound by orders and undertakings of confidentiality

propositions.text: This principle applies even more strongly to disclosure to third parties who are not charged.
propositions.quote: This principle must, a fortiori, apply to disclosure to interested third parties or their representatives, persons who do not face criminal charges

paragraphs.summary: The court finds CBC's position conflicts with precedent that informer privilege cannot be lifted for defence or third parties despite confidentiality undertakings.

propositions.text: No reason exists to depart from the law that maximizes disclosure but never compromises informer anonymity.
propositions.quote: we are not convinced that there is any reason to depart from the current state of the law, under which as much information as possible should be disclosed to interested third parties, but never any information that might compromise the police informer’s anonymity

propositions.text: CBC et al. consider the rule imperfect and want more information disclosed to third parties.
propositions.quote: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. may consider this rule imperfect or insufficient, insofar as the submissions made by interested third parties might be even more relevant if they had access to more information

propositions.text: The rule ensures informer privilege objectives and maximizes helpfulness of third party submissions.
propositions.quote: it is a rule that must be reiterated because it has the advantage of ensuring that the dual objectives underlying the informer privilege rule are achieved while at the same time maximizing the helpfulness of the submissions made by interested third parties

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects CBC's call for more disclosure, affirming the current law protects informer anonymity while allowing helpful third party submissions.

propositions.text: CBC et al. propose third parties be informed of the nature and reasons for non-disclosure to make arguments.
propositions.quote: if information that might tend to indirectly identify the informer cannot be disclosed to interested third parties, then these parties should at least be systematically apprised of both the nature of the information sought to be shielded from public view and the concrete reason for not disclosing the information to them

propositions.text: Attorney General of Ontario argues this endangers informer anonymity and overlooks that informer privilege leaves no room for balancing interests.
propositions.quote: this position seems to overlook the fact that the rationale for confidentiality orders in such cases — to protect informer privilege — leaves no room for a balancing of competing interests

propositions.text: The court agrees with Attorney General that systematic disclosure would endanger anonymity and limit judicial discretion.
propositions.quote: turning such disclosure into a systematic and inflexible rule might unduly tie the courts’ hands and, ultimately, limit their ability to render justice in each case

paragraphs.summary: CBC wants systematic disclosure of reasons for non-disclosure; the court agrees with Ontario that this risks anonymity and limits judicial discretion.

propositions.text: The court will explain how to apply Vancouver Sun's guiding rule when proceeding in camera to protect informer identity and accommodate open court principle.
propositions.quote: we will now explain what the application of the guiding rule from Vancouver Sun requires when proceeding in camera

propositions.text: Named Person was not convicted following a secret proceeding.
propositions.quote: Named Person was not convicted following a secret proceeding

paragraphs.summary: The court will explain applying Vancouver Sun in camera and clarifies Named Person was not convicted in a secret proceeding.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal's March 2022 redacted reasons led public to believe Named Person was convicted in a secret trial.
propositions.quote: led the public to believe that Named Person had been convicted following a secret criminal proceeding

propositions.text: Public concern was fueled by erroneous expression 'secret trial' repeated by media.
propositions.quote: Public concern and indignation were further fuelled by the use of the erroneous expression “secret trial”

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Court of Appeal's reasons and media caused public to wrongly believe Named Person was convicted in a secret trial.

propositions.text: Named Person was not convicted following a secret proceeding; Court of Appeal backtracked and linked in camera proceedings to stay motion.
propositions.quote: Named Person was not convicted following a secret criminal proceeding

propositions.text: Vancouver Sun procedure applied at trial begins publicly and remains public even if accused is informer.
propositions.quote: the claim to informer status is made in a proceeding that begins publicly through the filing of a criminal prosecution and that then generally moves forward publicly

propositions.text: Crown cannot presume accused will reveal informer status or raise related defence when initiating prosecution.
propositions.quote: the Crown, in fulfilling its absolute duty to keep the accused’s informer status confidential, cannot presume when it initiates criminal proceedings against the accused that the accused will agree to reveal their informer status to their counsel and will raise a defence related to that status

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Named Person's trial began publicly, Vancouver Sun procedure applies, and Crown cannot presume accused reveals informer status.

propositions.text: Proceeding began publicly and moved publicly until Named Person brought stay motion based on abusive conduct as informer.
propositions.quote: The proceeding against Named Person therefore began publicly through the filing of a criminal prosecution. It moved forward publicly until Named Person decided to bring a motion for a stay of proceedings

propositions.text: Judge held in camera hearing to verify informer status, then heard stay motion in camera, deciding no notice to third parties was appropriate.
propositions.quote: the judge held an in camera hearing to verify Named Person’s status as an informer... the judge correctly found that the motion for a stay of proceedings had to be heard in camera... decided that it was not appropriate to give notice to interested third parties

propositions.text: Judge's discretionary decision to not notify third parties was justified.
propositions.quote: a discretionary decision that was his to make and that was justified in this case

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the public start of proceedings, in camera verification and stay motion, and justifies judge's no-notice decision.

propositions.text: Judge and participants acted honestly and sincerely to protect anonymity.
propositions.quote: At all times, the judge and the justice system participants involved acted with honesty, integrity and a sincere desire to protect Named Person’s anonymity

propositions.text: Judge mistakenly thought complete concealment of in camera hearing and decision was necessary.
propositions.quote: the judge mistakenly thought that the only approach to be taken... was to completely conceal the existence of any in camera hearing

propositions.text: No need to leave stay motion off docket or without formal number; better procedure could accommodate open court and informer privilege.
propositions.quote: there was no need for the motion for a stay of proceedings to be left off the court’s docket and hearing roll and for no formal number to be assigned to it

paragraphs.summary: The court finds judge acted honestly but mistakenly concealed in camera hearing existence, and better procedure could balance openness and privilege.

propositions.text: When informer status is asserted in public proceeding and is central, total in camera proceeding is generally appropriate.
propositions.quote: The appropriate way to protect the informer’s anonymity will generally be to proceed totally in camera

propositions.text: Bastarache J. in Vancouver Sun contemplated total confidentiality in exceptional cases.
propositions.quote: such a degree of confidentiality may be required in exceptional cases like the present one was expressly contemplated by Bastarache J. in Vancouver Sun

paragraphs.summary: The court states total in camera proceedings are generally appropriate when informer status is central, as contemplated by Vancouver Sun.

propositions.text: Application of Vancouver Sun requires in camera proceedings be consistent with open court principle as much as possible.
propositions.quote: the application of the guiding rule from Vancouver Sun requires the presiding judge to do so in a manner that is as consistent as possible with the open court principle

propositions.text: Even in confidential cases, protecting anonymity while avoiding indefinite secrecy is essential and possible.
propositions.quote: it is possible — and we would go so far as to say essential — to protect the informer’s anonymity while still favouring confidentiality orders that do not entirely or indefinitely keep the existence of a hearing or judgment from the public

propositions.text: Compliance with Vancouver Sun and public confidence require creativity and administrative arrangements.
propositions.quote: what is in issue is compliance with the guiding rule from Vancouver Sun and the maintenance of public confidence in the administration of justice

paragraphs.summary: The court requires in camera proceedings to align with open court principle, protecting anonymity without indefinite secrecy, maintaining public confidence.

propositions.text: Minimum openness requires public disclosure of existence of in camera hearing and any decision rendered.
propositions.quote: at a minimum, the existence of the in camera hearing and of any decision rendered as a result will be made public

propositions.text: Some information including reasons for in camera may remain confidential; in extreme cases, hearing existence or judgment may be disclosed later or sealed.
propositions.quote: it may well be that a range of information... will have to be kept confidential... it is also possible, in an extreme case, that the existence of the in camera hearing will not be made public until after the fact

propositions.text: Rarely is indefinite confidentiality of hearing existence compatible with protecting informer anonymity.
propositions.quote: we have difficulty imagining a single scenario in which revealing the mere existence of an in camera hearing and of any decision rendered as a result is incompatible with the protection of an informer’s anonymity

propositions.text: Minimum openness enables third parties to seek review and prevents judiciary avoiding accountability.
propositions.quote: Such a minimum threshold for openness also has added importance in enabling interested third parties to file a motion for review of the confidentiality orders and thus to prevent the judiciary from avoiding any form of accountability

paragraphs.summary: The court mandates public disclosure of in camera hearing existence and decisions, with limited confidentiality, to ensure accountability and protect anonymity.

propositions.text: At least one approach exists to avoid indefinite secrecy of in camera hearing and decisions.
propositions.quote: In a case like this one, at least one approach can be taken to ensure that the existence of an in camera hearing and of any decision rendered as a result is not kept from the public entirely or indefinitely

paragraphs.summary: The court states there is at least one approach to avoid indefinite secrecy of in camera hearings and decisions.

propositions.text: Creating a parallel sealed proceeding with its own record number can protect informer privilege and allow public docketing and redacted judgments.
propositions.quote: This approach involves creating a parallel proceeding that is completely separate from the public proceeding in which informer privilege is initially invoked

propositions.text: Example from B. (A.) case where in camera hearings and redacted public judgment protected informer identity.
propositions.quote: As an illustration of what such a public judgment might look like, consider what was done in B. (A.)

propositions.text: Trial held entirely in camera with pseudonyms and redacted reasons to protect informer identity.
propositions.quote: The trial, in its entirety, was held in camera... Only in this way can AB’s identity as a confidential informant be protected

paragraphs.summary: The court explains creating a parallel sealed proceeding allows public docketing and redacted judgments, illustrated by B. (A.) case.

propositions.text: Judge must consider what information must remain confidential to prevent linking parallel and public proceedings.
propositions.quote: the presiding judge must consider what information has to remain confidential in the context of that new proceeding in order to prevent the two proceedings from being linked to each other

propositions.text: Confidential details may include judge, counsel, prosecutor identities, judicial district, or dates to avoid indirect identification.
propositions.quote: the protection of informer privilege may require that one or more of the following details be kept confidential: the judge’s identity, the identity of the parties’ counsel, the prosecutor’s identity, the judicial district or the date of a proceeding or judgment

propositions.text: Examples of confidentiality measures from prior cases cited.
propositions.quote: see, e.g., Her Majesty the Queen v. Named Person A, 2017 ABQB 552... R. v. X and Y, 2012 BCSC 325

paragraphs.summary: The court requires judges to keep certain details confidential to prevent linking parallel and public proceedings, citing prior cases.

propositions.text: Judge must consider measures like changing judge or venue to accommodate open court principle without compromising anonymity.
propositions.quote: the judge must then ask whether measures can be contemplated to accommodate the open court principle

propositions.text: If less intrusive measures are not possible, judge must keep information confidential and off public record.
propositions.quote: if the circumstances do not allow for measures that interfere less with court openness, the judge must order that this information be kept confidential

paragraphs.summary: The court instructs judges to consider less intrusive measures to protect anonymity and keep confidential information off public record if necessary.

propositions.text: Judge must consider if decision from parallel in camera proceeding can be made public with redactions.
propositions.quote: the presiding judge must consider whether the decision can be made public, subject to the redaction of confidential information

propositions.text: Exceptional cases may require sealing judgments despite parallel proceeding.
propositions.quote: it is always possible that exceptional cases may arise in which the protection of a police informer’s identity will require that a judgment rendered following an in camera hearing be kept under seal

paragraphs.summary: The court requires judges to consider public redacted release of decisions but allows sealing in exceptional cases.

propositions.text: Parallel proceeding allows public knowledge of in camera hearing existence and decisions, usually with redactions.
propositions.quote: the creation of a parallel proceeding makes it possible to disclose, at a minimum, the existence of the in camera hearing and of any decision rendered as a result

propositions.text: Public can learn of hearings via docket or hearing roll and notice of sealed judgments.
propositions.quote: The public can learn of their existence through the court’s docket or hearing roll and, in appropriate circumstances, through notice that a sealed judgment has been delivered

propositions.text: Parallel proceeding informs public of issues ruled on and reasons for in camera proceedings.
propositions.quote: the creation of a parallel proceeding has the advantage of making the public aware of the decisions rendered at trial and, where applicable, on appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court explains parallel proceedings enable public awareness of in camera hearings and decisions, preserving transparency with confidentiality.

propositions.text: Parallel proceeding allows public notice of in camera proceedings so third parties can make submissions on openness.
propositions.quote: This approach has the advantage of... providing public notice of a proceeding in which an accused invokes informer privilege and of the court’s intention to proceed in camera

propositions.text: Presiding judge may take special measures to prevent linking parallel and public proceedings before allowing third party submissions.
propositions.quote: the presiding judge, before allowing interested third parties to make their submissions, may have to take special measures to prevent the proceedings from being linked to each other

paragraphs.summary: The court states parallel proceedings can provide public notice for third party submissions, with measures to prevent linking proceedings.

propositions.text: Solution allows disclosure of minimum information to third parties to file motions for review of confidentiality orders
propositions.quote: this solution makes it possible to disclose at least a minimum amount of information to interested third parties, including the news media, that wish to file a motion for review of the confidentiality orders

propositions.text: This reduces risk that news outlets aware of in camera hearing cannot make helpful submissions
propositions.quote: This lessens the risk of the unfortunate occurrence where a news outlet that has become aware of the in camera hearing is unable to make helpful submissions because it is impossible for the court to provide it with a minimum amount of information

paragraphs.summary: Court finds solution allows disclosure of minimum information to third parties, reducing risk news outlets cannot make helpful submissions.

propositions.text: Trial judge could and should have created a parallel proceeding separate from the public criminal proceeding
propositions.quote: the trial judge could and, in retrospect, should have made an order to that effect while creating a parallel proceeding completely separate from the criminal proceeding

propositions.text: Parallel proceeding would have its own record number and could be on court docket with redacted judgment released
propositions.quote: That parallel proceeding would have had its own record number... could have been on the court’s docket and hearing roll, and a redacted version of the judgment on the motion could have been released

propositions.text: Court emphasizes this approach to prevent recurrence of similar situations
propositions.quote: we are of the view that it is important to emphasize this to ensure that this type of situation does not occur again in the future

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge should have created a parallel proceeding with redacted judgment to avoid recurrence of similar issues.

propositions.text: Court will now address Court of Appeal’s dismissal of appellants’ motions and upholding of sealing identifying information
propositions.quote: we will now address the Court of Appeal’s decision to dismiss the appellants’ motions for review of its confidentiality orders and to uphold the sealing of all information that might tend to identify Named Person

paragraphs.summary: Court states it will address Court of Appeal’s dismissal of motions and sealing orders.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal correctly opened record and made public redacted judgment allowing Named Person’s appeal
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal’s decision to open a record in the court office and to make public a redacted version of its judgment... was correct

propositions.text: These measures were necessary to accommodate open court principle and democratic ideals
propositions.quote: These measures were necessary both to accommodate the open court principle and to promote the democratic ideals that define it

propositions.text: Decision disclosed existence of in camera proceedings and abuse of process against Named Person
propositions.quote: the decision has the merit of disclosing to the public the existence of in camera proceedings as well as the abuse of process committed against Named Person

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Court of Appeal correctly opened record and disclosed in camera proceedings and abuse of process.

propositions.text: Appellants challenge Court of Appeal’s refusal to lift confidentiality orders fully or partially
propositions.quote: the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. are challenging the Court of Appeal’s refusal to lift its confidentiality orders in whole or in part

propositions.text: Appellants ask Court to ensure redactions protecting Named Person’s anonymity are justified and minimally impair open court principle
propositions.quote: They are asking this Court to ensure that the redaction undertaken by the Court of Appeal... is justified and that it impairs the open court principle as little as possible

propositions.text: Appellants argue Court of Appeal’s refusal to partially unseal appeal record is unjustified
propositions.quote: the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al. argue that the Court of Appeal’s repeated refusal to partially unseal the appeal record is unjustified

propositions.text: Court of Appeal should have unsealed appeal record consistent with redacted public judgment disclosing excerpts from trial judgment and police transcripts
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal should, at a minimum, have unsealed the appeal record in a manner that corresponded to the redaction of the public version of its judgment

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Court of Appeal wrongly refused to partially unseal appeal record and redactions should be minimal.

propositions.text: Only problematic aspect of confidentiality orders is refusal to partially unseal appeal record to make redacted trial judgment public
propositions.quote: only one aspect of the confidentiality orders... is problematic... the court’s decision not to partially unseal the appeal record in order to make a redacted version of the trial judgment public

paragraphs.summary: Court finds only problematic confidentiality order aspect is refusal to partially unseal appeal record for redacted trial judgment.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal did not unduly shield information in its judgments from public view
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal did not unduly shield information in those judgments from public view

propositions.text: Circumstances required heavy redactions to protect Named Person’s anonymity
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal had no choice but to redact its judgments as heavily as it did

propositions.text: Named Person appeared publicly initially; informer-police relationship central to stay motion; other confidential circumstances exist
propositions.quote: Named Person initially appeared in a public criminal proceeding and that the informer‑police relationship was central to Named Person’s motion for a stay of proceedings, but there are also other particular and unusual circumstances

propositions.text: Court had duty to keep confidential Named Person’s identity and related details to avoid risk of compromising anonymity
propositions.quote: Court of Appeal had a duty to keep confidential Named Person’s name, the identity of the trial court and judge... Otherwise, there would have been a real risk... of compromising Named Person’s identity

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Court of Appeal properly redacted judgments to protect Named Person’s anonymity and had duty to do so.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal erred in refusing to make public a redacted version of the trial judgment protecting anonymity
propositions.quote: it erred in refusing to make public a version of the trial judgment that was redacted in such a way as to protect Named Person’s anonymity

propositions.text: Redacting trial judgment was feasible and would accommodate open court principle
propositions.quote: this was an entirely feasible undertaking that would have accommodated the open court principle

propositions.text: Court of Appeal correctly refused to partially unseal rest of appeal record due to high risk of compromising anonymity
propositions.quote: we agree with the Court of Appeal that partial unsealing carried with it too high a risk of error... The Court of Appeal did not err in refusing to undertake such an unsealing exercise

propositions.text: Principle of caution requires sealing rest of appeal record to protect anonymity
propositions.quote: The principle of caution that must guide the courts in protecting Named Person’s anonymity required that the rest of the appeal record be kept under seal

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Court of Appeal erred by not releasing redacted trial judgment but correctly sealed rest of appeal record to protect anonymity.

propositions.text: Named Person was not convicted following a secret criminal proceeding
propositions.quote: Named Person was not convicted following a secret criminal proceeding

propositions.text: Controversy arose from Court of Appeal’s use of 'secret trial' expression and gap between public knowledge and reality
propositions.quote: controversy... arose after the release... in which it denounced the holding of a “secret trial” is unfortunate and could have been avoided

propositions.text: Trial judge should have created parallel proceeding separate from public criminal proceeding
propositions.quote: it could have been avoided if the trial judge had proceeded in camera by creating a parallel proceeding completely separate from the criminal proceeding

propositions.text: Use of 'secret trial' expression was inaccurate, needlessly alarming, and has no basis in Canadian law
propositions.quote: this expression is needlessly alarming and has no basis in Canadian law

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no secret trial occurred; controversy arose from inaccurate 'secret trial' expression and trial judge’s failure to create parallel proceeding.

propositions.text: Vancouver Sun procedure requires protecting informer privilege while minimizing impairment of open court principle
propositions.quote: importance of rigorously applying its guiding rule requiring a court to protect informer privilege while minimizing... impairment of the open court principle

propositions.text: Courts must be flexible and creative to maintain public confidence and respect for rule of law
propositions.quote: courts must be flexible and creative. What is in issue is the maintenance of public confidence in the administration of justice and respect for the rule of law

paragraphs.summary: Court emphasizes Vancouver Sun procedure and need for courts to protect informer privilege while minimizing open court impairment.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal was in difficult position as appeal did not relate to trial judge’s confidentiality orders
propositions.quote: it was in a difficult position, as it had before it an appeal that did not relate in any way to the trial judge’s confidentiality orders

propositions.text: Court of Appeal correctly championed open court principle by opening record and making public redacted judgment
propositions.quote: we can only commend its decision to proactively champion the open court principle... by opening a record... and making public a redacted version of its judgment

propositions.text: Given circumstances, Court of Appeal correctly dismissed motions for total or partial disclosure
propositions.quote: Given the particular circumstances of this case... it was therefore correct to dismiss the motions for total or partial disclosure

propositions.text: Court of Appeal erred in sealing entire appeal record; should have made public redacted trial judgment
propositions.quote: it erred in upholding its order that the entire appeal record be sealed. It should have made public a redacted version of the trial judgment

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Court of Appeal was correct to champion open court principle but erred by sealing entire appeal record instead of releasing redacted trial judgment.

propositions.text: All justice system participants acted in good faith and with integrity to protect Named Person’s anonymity
propositions.quote: there is no doubt that all of the justice system participants involved were in good faith and acted with integrity

propositions.text: Decision will guide trial judges to accommodate open court principle when proceeding in camera
propositions.quote: We believe that this decision will be helpful and will guide trial judges who must proceed in camera, in order to ensure that they accommodate the open court principle

paragraphs.summary: Court finds all participants acted in good faith and decision will guide trial judges to respect open court principle.

propositions.text: Court allows appeals in part and remands to Quebec Court of Appeal to make public redacted trial judgment after consultation
propositions.quote: the Court allows the appeals in part and remands the case to the Quebec Court of Appeal so that it can make public a redacted version of the trial judgment

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeals in part and remands for public release of redacted trial judgment after consultation.
